steps.text: thanks for being here. let's spend one gentle minute.
picture someone dear having a rough day. what would they need to hear?

steps.prompt: pick any that fit, or none.
options: it makes sense this is hard
you don't have to be perfect
steps.reply: those are kind. now let's point them inward.

steps.prompt: now the same kindness, inward, using your own name. slowly, out loud if possible. tap the one tried.
lines: {name}, it makes sense this is hard.
steps.reply: notice how that landed. that's the voice we're growing.

steps.text: compared to the usual inner talk, how was that?

options.label: softer
options.reply: that softness is the whole point. it's there any time.

options.label: strange
options.reply: of course. kind words inward can feel unfamiliar. they get easier with practice.

options.label: about the same
options.reply: that's okay too. sometimes it takes a few tries, and the right words.

steps.text: self-compassion became a research topic in 2003, when psychologist kristin neff found a way to measure it. since then, hundreds of studies have looked at how people treat themselves on hard days.
steps.evidence: the measure is well established; what it predicts is still being studied

ideas: it makes sense this is hard.
one step at a time is enough.
this is one hard day, not a whole life.

steps.text: kindness inward isn't going easy. across many studies, people who treat themselves kindly tend to report greater well-being.
steps.evidence: moderate (a consistent link across 79 samples; mostly not proof of cause)

steps.text: tonight, say the kind line once, using your own name.

grounding.idea: self-compassion goes along with greater well-being
grounding.source: Zessin, Dickhäuser & Garbade, 2015, Applied Psychology: Health and Well-Being

grounding.idea: talking to yourself as "you" or by name reduces distress under stress
grounding.source: Kross et al., 2014, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
